title: ACT Pronoun Agreement and Clear Reference
summary: Matching pronouns to singular and plural antecedents, keeping one/you consistent, and fixing ambiguous, missing and vague references (they say, this, which) — with worked examples and an ACT-style quiz.

blocks.text: A pronoun (it, they, its, their, this, which…) is a short word that stands for a noun. That noun is called its **antecedent**. Every pronoun must do two things: **agree** with its antecedent in number (singular or plural) and person, and point **clearly** to one antecedent that is actually in the passage. ACT English tests both. The errors are easy to miss because, when you read quickly, your brain fills in the meaning for you.
What this question type tests

Pronoun agreement and reference belong to **Conventions of Standard English**, which is **38–43%** of the 40 scored English questions (shared with punctuation, sentence structure and the other usage topics). An underlined pronoun has choices such as **it / they / its / their / this / the museum**. Very often one choice replaces the pronoun with a **noun** — that choice is the correct one when the pronoun is unclear.
For every underlined pronoun, do two checks:

items: **Find the antecedent.** Go back in the sentence (or the sentence before) and point to the exact noun the pronoun replaces.

**Check the match.** Singular noun → it / its / he / she / this. Plural noun → they / them / their / these. If you cannot point to **one** noun — because there are two possibilities or none at all — the pronoun is wrong, and the answer is usually the choice that names the noun.

blocks.text: Rule 1: Singular antecedents take singular pronouns
The commonest ACT error is **their** or **they** used for a singular thing. Look especially for these singular antecedents:

rows: a company, a school, a university, a museum
The company raised **their** prices.
The company raised **its** prices.
a team, a committee, a band, a family, a government
The committee announced **their** decision on Monday.
The committee announced **its** decision on Monday.
a city, a country, a river
Egypt depends on the Nile for most of **their** water.
Egypt depends on the Nile for most of **its** water.
each / every / either / neither + thing
Each of the bridges has **their** own name.
Each of the bridges has **its** own name.
one of the + plural noun
One of the old trams still has **their** wooden seats.
One of the old trams still has **its** wooden seats.

blocks.text: These words agree with the **verb** too: if the sentence says “the team **is**”, the pronoun must be “**its**”, not “their”. The ACT is written in American English, where a group acting as one unit is singular.

**People words** such as everyone, anybody, each student, a person: modern Standard English often uses “they/their” for one person whose gender is not stated (✓ Each student must bring **their** own calculator). Traditional style uses “his or her”. Because both are accepted today, the ACT does not normally make that the only difference between choices. What it does test is a singular **thing** or **organisation** with “they/their” — that is always wrong.

**Plural antecedents take plural pronouns:** ✗ The pyramids are famous for **its** size. ✓ The pyramids are famous for **their** size. Two nouns joined by **and** are plural: ✓ The mosque and the church kept **their** old doors. With **or / nor**, the pronoun agrees with the nearer noun: ✓ Neither the teachers nor the principal gave **her** opinion.

blocks.title: its / it’s and their / they’re / there
blocks.text: Agreement questions often mix in apostrophe traps. **its** = belonging to it; **it’s** = it is / it has. **their** = belonging to them; **they’re** = they are; **there** = a place / there is. Choose the right **number** first (its vs their), then the right **spelling**.
Rule 2: Stay consistent — one, you, we
When a passage talks about people in general, it may use **one**, **you** or **we**. Whichever it starts with, it must keep. Switching person in the middle of a sentence or paragraph is an error.

rows: If **one** practises every day, **you** will improve quickly.
If **one** practises every day, **one** will improve quickly. / If **you** practise every day, **you** will improve quickly.
When **we** visit the desert at night, **you** can see thousands of stars.
When **we** visit the desert at night, **we** can see thousands of stars.
A **student** should check **your** answers twice.
A **student** should check **his or her** answers twice. / **Students** should check **their** answers twice.

blocks.text: To choose, look at the rest of the passage, especially the **non-underlined** pronouns. The underlined pronoun must match the ones you cannot change.

blocks.title: الضمير لازم يرجع على اسم واحد
blocks.text: اسأل نفسك: الضمير ده راجع على أنهي اسم بالظبط؟ لو الاسم مفرد (الشركة، الفريق، المدينة، المتحف) يبقى it / its مش they / their. ولو الجملة بدأت بـ you كمّل بـ you، ولو بدأت بـ one كمّل بـ one — ماينفعش تغيّر في نص الكلام.
Rule 3: Ambiguous pronouns — two possible antecedents

If a pronoun could refer to **two different nouns**, the reader cannot be sure who or what is meant. Grammar is not enough here; the meaning must be clear. The fix is to replace the pronoun with the noun it means.

rows: When Mona showed her sister the photograph, **she** started to cry.
Mona or her sister?
When Mona showed her sister the photograph, **her sister** started to cry.
The engineers argued with the builders because **they** wanted to finish early.
engineers or builders?
…because **the builders** wanted to finish early.
The cup fell off the shelf, and **it** broke.
the cup or the shelf?
The cup fell off the shelf and broke.
Sami told Ali that **his** bike had been stolen.
Sami’s bike or Ali’s?
Sami told Ali, “**Your** bike has been stolen.” / Sami told Ali that **Ali’s** bike had been stolen.

blocks.text: Notice that the ACT’s correct answer is often **longer** than the pronoun. Usually a shorter answer is better on this test, but **clarity beats length**: choose the noun when the pronoun is ambiguous.
Rule 4: Pronouns with no antecedent
A pronoun needs a real noun in the passage. These are the patterns the ACT uses:

items: **“They say / they told me” with no group named.** ✗ At the clinic, **they** told me to rest. ✓ At the clinic, **a nurse** told me to rest. ✗ **They** say the old bridge will be closed. ✓ **City officials** say the old bridge will be closed.
**“It says” for a written source.** ✗ In the article, **it** says the river is cleaner. ✓ **The article** says the river is cleaner.

**The antecedent is only an adjective or a possessive.** ✗ In **Nadia’s** report, **she** argues for more parks. (“Nadia’s” describes “report”; it cannot be the antecedent.) ✓ In **her** report, **Nadia** argues for more parks. ✗ I visited a **pottery** workshop, and now I want to learn **it**. (“pottery” is only describing “workshop”.) ✓ …and now I want to learn **pottery**.
**The noun is only implied.** ✗ My uncle is a doctor, so I want to study **it**. (“it” = medicine, which is not in the sentence.) ✓ My uncle is a doctor, so I want to study **medicine**.

blocks.text: Rule 5: “This” and “which” for a whole idea

Writers often use **this**, **that** or **which** to point back to a whole action or idea instead of a single noun. When only **one** idea could be meant, the reader understands. When two or more ideas come before it, the reference is **vague**, and the clear choice adds a noun: **this delay**, **this change**, **this decision**.

rows: The city cut the number of buses on our route and raised the ticket price. **This** made many students late for school.
…**This reduction in buses** made many students late for school.
Laila missed the bus, and the exam started early, **which** meant she arrived after the first question.
Laila missed the bus, and the exam started early. **These two problems** meant she arrived after the first question.
The scientists collected the samples. **These** shows the water is safe.
The scientists collected the samples. **These samples** show the water is safe.

blocks.text: Also check agreement: **this / that** for one idea or a singular noun; **these / those** for plural nouns. ✗ “This results” ✓ “These results”.

blocks.title: this لوحدها ممكن تبقى مش واضحة
blocks.text: لو الجملة اللي قبل كده فيها فكرتين، كلمة This لوحدها مش هتوضح بنتكلم عن أنهي فكرة. الحل: حط اسم بعدها، زي This decision أو This delay. وفي الامتحان، الاختيار اللي بيكتب الاسم بدل الضمير غالبًا هو الصح لما الضمير يكون مش واضح.
Worked examples
Each example is part of an ACT-style essay. The underlined portion is shown in **bold**.
**Worked example 1.** “The Egyptian Museum in Tahrir reopened last month after two years of repairs, and **their** new lighting makes the gold masks glow.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) its
C) it’s
D) they’re

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** The new lighting belongs to the museum (singular), so the singular possessive “its” is needed.
**A** is plural; it seems to agree with “years” or “repairs”, the nearest plural nouns, but the lighting belongs to the museum. The trap is the nearest plural noun.
**C** means “it is”. **D** means “they are”. Neither is a possessive.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2.** “When Mona showed her younger sister the old photograph of their grandfather, **she** started to cry.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) her sister
C) they
D) it

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** “She” could mean Mona or her sister — two possible antecedents. Naming the person removes the ambiguity.
**A** is the ambiguous pronoun.
**C** is plural and still unclear.
**D** refers to the photograph, which cannot cry.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3.** “My first visit to the eye clinic was confusing. At the reception desk, **they** told me to wait, but nobody explained for how long.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) a receptionist
C) it
D) she

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** “They” has no antecedent: no group of people has been named. “A receptionist” gives the action a clear subject.
**A** is a pronoun with no antecedent (“the clinic” is one place, not “they”).
**C** would make the desk or the clinic speak.
**D** is also a pronoun with no antecedent: no woman has been mentioned.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4.** “If one wants to learn Japanese, **you** should begin with the two simple alphabets before studying the Chinese characters.”
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) they
C) one
D) we

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** The sentence begins with “one”, which is not underlined and cannot change, so the pronoun must stay “one”.
**A** and **D** shift from “one” to another person (you, we).
**B** is plural and refers to no one in the sentence.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **their / they for one organisation or thing:** the company, the team, the city, the museum, each bridge → it / its.
**Nearest plural noun:** “the museum … after two years of repairs … their lighting” — find the real owner, not the closest noun.
**Two possible antecedents:** he, she, they or it could mean two nouns → name the noun.
**They say / it says / at the clinic they…:** a pronoun that refers to no one in the passage.
**Possessive or adjective as antecedent:** “In Nadia’s report, she…”, “a pottery class … learn it”.
**Person shift:** one → you, we → you in the same sentence or paragraph.
**Vague this / which:** two ideas before it → add a noun (this delay).

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Put your finger on the antecedent. Can’t find exactly one? Choose the answer that names the noun.
Singular thing or group → it / its / this. Plural → they / their / these.
Check the pronouns you cannot change (not underlined) and match the underlined one to them.
If the choices are NO CHANGE, a pronoun and a noun, ask whether the original is really clear before choosing the shorter answer.

blocks.text: Practice
Two ACT-style essays with 5 questions each, all on pronoun agreement and clear reference. The numbers in brackets match the question numbers.

blocks.title: Pronoun Agreement and Reference quiz
blocks.intro: Two ACT-style essays with 5 questions each. For every underlined pronoun, point to its antecedent first: one noun, the right number, clearly in the passage.

questions.p:
Chairs from the Sea

In 2015, two engineering graduates in Alexandria started a small company that turns old fishing nets into outdoor chairs. At first, the company had no factory of __their__ [1] own, so the founders rented a corner of a car repair garage near the harbor.

When the founders first met the fishermen of Abu Qir, __they__ [2] explained that worn-out nets were usually burned on the beach or simply thrown into the sea. The founders offered to buy every old net the boats could bring them. Within a year, the garage was so full of nylon that the mechanics had to park their cars in the street.

The first chairs were heavy and gray. In the city's newspaper, __they__ [3] described them as "ugly but impossible to break." Still, each chair keeps about two kilograms of nylon out of the water. __These__ [4] has convinced several hotels on the north coast to buy them for their gardens.

As one of the founders likes to say, if you want to clean the sea, __you have__ [5] to start on the beach.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: The antecedent is “the company”, one organisation, so the singular possessive “its” is needed. A is plural; B means “it is”; D is a place word, not a possessive.

questions.p:
A Forest Behind the Sports Field

Last year, our school's environment club decided to plant a small forest of native trees behind the sports field. The club meets every Tuesday, and at __their__ [6] first meeting of the year, the members voted to begin in March.

The seedlings arrived in a truck from a nursery in Fayoum. Although __it__ [7] looked like thin brown sticks, each one already had healthy roots. Mr. Fathy, our biology teacher, worked with the school gardener, Am Saber, to choose the species, and __he__ [8] insisted on trees that need very little water.

If you have never planted a tree, __you__ [9] might be surprised by how deep the hole must be. We dug forty holes in two days, and our hands were covered in blisters by the end. Twelve of the young trees died during the first hot summer, but the rest survived.

Today the trees are taller than we are. __They say__ [10] that a forest needs about ten years to look like a real forest, so the club plans to keep watering until we graduate and long after.
questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: The antecedent is “The club”, which acts as one group (“The club meets”), so the singular possessive “its” is needed. A is plural; C means “it is”; D means “they are”.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Every pronoun needs one clear antecedent and must match it in number: company, team, city, museum → it / its.
Keep the same person all the way through: one … one, you … you, we … we.
Two possible antecedents? Replace the pronoun with the noun, even if the answer is longer.
“They say”, “it says”, and pronouns pointing to a possessive or an adjective have no real antecedent.
Vague this / which after two ideas → add a noun: this delay, this decision.
